```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

Supplemental equations + semi toy example calculating growth rates and transmission advantages logistic and multinomial variant nowcast models. 

#1.Simple Logistic growth

##1a. Logistic growth equation
Adopted from Chen et al., 2021 and Althaus et al., 
$$
p_v(t) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\beta(t - t_0)}} \tag{1a.}
$$
Where $p_v(t)$ is the proportion of the variant at time $t$ days, and $\beta variant$ is the exponential growth rate and $t0$ is the sigmoid midpoint.


###Example
We can use NLS to directly input the function and have it estimate parameters. 
```{r}
#read in PANGO sequences 
pangonum <- read_tsv("~/growthadvantagecompare/sequences_static/global.tsv") %>% 
  mutate(variant = "pango") %>% 
  rename(name = clade)

pangototn_usa <- pangonum %>% filter(location == "USA") %>% 
  group_by(date) %>% summarise(totn = sum(sequences)) %>% 
  mutate("variant" = "pango")

#proportions of each clade and pango lineage by day 
pangoprops_usa <- left_join(pangototn_usa, pangonum %>% filter(location == "USA"), by = "date") %>% 
 mutate(pangoprop = sequences/totn) 

#plot B.1.1.7

pangoprops_usa %>%
  filter(location == "USA", name == "B.1.1.7", date > as.Date("2020-08-20")) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  filter(date <= date[which.max(pangoprop)]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(date, pangoprop)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = totn), alpha = 0.2, colour = "#2166ac") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion of sequences", size = "Total sequences",
       title = "B.1.1.7 in the USA, rise to peak beginning 2020-08-20") +
  theme_minimal()

#Convert to useable df 
pangoprops_input<- pangoprops_usa %>%
  filter(location == "USA", name == "B.1.1.7", date > as.Date("2020-08-20")) %>% 
   filter(date <= date[which.max(pangoprop)]) %>% #also filter date to only include max proportion date
 mutate(t = as.numeric(date - min(date))) %>% 
  arrange(t) %>% 
  select(date, t, name, totn, pangoprop)

#Write the function

#p_v(t) = 1/ (1 + exp(-beta * (t - t0))
#p(-Vt) is our input ie pangoprop or the proportion of variant B117 at time t, or p(day)
#we guess that the beta (growth rate) is .05, this is where the function starts searching 

nfit <- nls(pangoprop ~ 1 / (1 + exp(-beta * (t - t0))),
            data    = pangoprops_input,
            start   = list(beta = 0.05, t0 = max(pangoprops_input$t) / 2), 
            weights = totn)

#Model outputs

coef(nfit)                 
beta  <- coef(nfit)[["beta"]] #so we get growth to be .036 per day, this is about half what chen and washington et al., get, one of the problems is that with incomplete variant information, the logistic functions assume that the growing variant will always reach 100%, which overestimates the growth rate 

t0 <- coef(nfit)[["t0"]]

t_grid<- seq(0, max(pangoprops_input$t, by = 1)) #making a grid of times using the t from our data

#lets plug these back into a function and plot the fit 

logistic_fun_so_fun <- function(beta, t, t0){
  
  return(1 / (1 + exp(-beta * (t - t0))))
  
}

fit_df <- data.frame(
  t    = t_grid,
  date = min(pangoprops_input$date) + t_grid,
  fit  = logistic_fun_so_fun(beta = beta, t = t_grid, t0 = t0)
)


ggplot(pangoprops_input, aes(date, pangoprop)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = totn), alpha = 0.4, colour = "#2166ac") +
  geom_line(data = fit_df, aes(date, fit), linewidth = 1, colour = "#b2182b") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = min(pangoprops_input$date) + t0,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion of sequences", size = "Total sequences",
       title = "B.1.1.7 in the USA with logistic fit",
       subtitle = sprintf("a = %.3f per day; dashed line = 50%% (t0)", a)) +
  theme_minimal()
```


##1b. Logistic growth advantage 
Assuming a fixed generation time of $g$, the transmission advantage, or $\Delta_v$ is the $R_t$ of the novel variant over all other variants ie $R_tnovel/R_tbackground$

Chen et al., 2021 uses this parameterization, as do Abousamra et al ., 2024 in the multinomial expansion.

$$
\Delta_v = e^{\beta g} = \frac{R_{t,\text{novel}}}{R_{t,\text{background}}} \tag{1b.}
$$
###Example
```{r}

deltav_fun <- function(beta, g){
  exp(beta*g)
}

#Lets choose the most generation time most recently estimated (even though this is probably a bad assumption)
#Hart, W. S. et al.,2022

g <- 5.5

delta_b117 <- deltav_fun(beta = beta, g = g)

delta_b117

#B117 is 1.22 times as transmissible as circulating background variants 
```
